---
title: "Practice: account for carbonyl addition one step at a time"
---

Allow 90 minutes. Colour or label the oxygen atoms so their identities remain
visible through each mechanism. Use explicit proton donors and acceptors.
The point is to understand the recurring pattern, not memorise every carbonyl
reagent. Review the [alcohol reduction](../alcohols-redox/exercise.qmd) for the
same addition → proton-transfer pattern with a different nucleophile.

## 1. Partial charge is not formal charge

Draw ethanal, CH₃CHO, with its carbonyl oxygen lone pairs. Mark the direction
of bond polarity and describe the geometry at carbon. Does δ+ at carbon mean
it is already a carbon atom with formal charge +1? Why can a nucleophile
attack carbon rather than the electron-rich oxygen in the selected addition?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The oxygen attracts electron density, leaving carbon partially electron-poor.
Carbonyl carbon is approximately trigonal planar, with three bond directions.
Both atoms have formal charge zero in the ordinary neutral Lewis structure;
partial charge describes uneven electron density. The nucleophile donates a
pair to the electron-poor carbon while the C=O π pair moves to oxygen,
making a chemically valid four-single-bond carbon centre.
:::

## 2. Base-catalysed hydration with an atom label

Label ethanal's oxygen A. Label the oxygen of attacking OH⁻ as B. Draw hydroxide
addition and then proton transfer from water. In the hydrate, which O came
from carbonyl and which from hydroxide? Why is hydroxide a catalyst in the
net transformation even though a hydroxide ion appears in the first step?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
After the first step, A is O⁻ and B is OH. Which species can supply H to A,
and which species remains after that donor has lost H⁺?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The first product is CH₃CH(OH-B)(O-A⁻). The B lone pair forms C–O-B while
the C=O-A π pair moves onto A. Water then donates H⁺ to A and becomes OH⁻.
Both A and B are OH in the hydrate CH₃CH(OH)₂, but their tracked identities
remain distinct in this drawing. Hydroxide is used and regenerated overall;
net hydration is ethanal + water ⇌ hydrate. The mechanism does not by itself
prove that the hydrate dominates the equilibrium mixture.
:::

## 3. Acid-catalysed hemiacetal formation

Start with ethanal and methanol. Label the carbonyl oxygen A and methanol
oxygen B. Draw three elementary stages: protonation of A using hydronium;
attack by methanol at carbon with the C=O π pair moving to A; removal of the
extra proton from B by water. Give formal charges after each stage.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Protonating A gives CH₃CH=O-AH⁺ plus water. Methanol O-B attacks carbon,
giving CH₃CH(OH-A)(O-B⁺HCH₃); A now has two single bonds and is neutral,
while B has three single bonds and charge +1. Water removes the B proton,
giving CH₃CH(OH-A)(O-BCH₃) and hydronium. The final product is a hemiacetal:
OH and OCH₃ are on the same carbon. The acid catalyst is regenerated.
:::

## 4. Distinguish the product classes

For each structure, circle the carbon of interest and classify it as an
aldehyde, hydrate, hemiacetal or acetal:

- CH₃CHO
- CH₃CH(OH)₂
- CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃
- CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂

Which difference would make it incorrect to call a hemiacetal an acetal?
For the net acid-catalysed equilibrium CH₃CHO + 2 CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃CH(OCH₃)₂ + H₂O,
predict the direction favoured by adding excess water. Explain the role
of acid separately from the effect of changing water concentration.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The listed classes are aldehyde, hydrate, hemiacetal and acetal, respectively.
A hemiacetal has one OH and one OR; an acetal has two OR groups on the same
carbon. Excess water can favour hydrolysis toward aldehyde and methanol.
Acid catalyses the interconversion and is regenerated; it does not change
the equilibrium constant for the same net reaction under the same conditions.
Converting a hemiacetal to an acetal requires additional activation, loss of
water, alcohol addition and proton transfer, not a single unexplained swap.
:::

## 5. Build a ring without losing an atom

Draw the chain HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO (5-hydroxypentanal). Show how its terminal
alcohol oxygen can attack the aldehyde carbon through the same chemical
pattern. Draw the neutral cyclic hemiacetal after proton transfers. Count
the ring atoms and compare molecular formula before and after. Is water
lost in the net chain → cyclic hemiacetal transformation?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The ring contains the attacking terminal oxygen, four methylene carbons and
the original aldehyde carbon: six ring atoms. The original carbonyl oxygen
becomes OH on that carbon. The molecular formula C₅H₁₀O₂ is unchanged; no
water molecule is lost in net hemiacetal cyclisation. The oxygen that forms
the ring is the original terminal alcohol oxygen. This is an organic
structure argument that also helps explain why some sugars can form rings.
:::

## 6. Prepare for acyl chemistry

Compare CH₃CHO and CH₃C(=O)OCH₃. Both have an electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
What group is bonded to that carbon in the ester that could participate in
an appropriate addition–elimination pathway? Why would treating H⁻ as an
ordinary leaving group from an aldehyde be a poor explanation of addition?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The ester has OCH₃ attached to the acyl carbon; under appropriate conditions,
an oxygen-based group can depart after addition and suitable proton transfers.
The aldehyde has H in that position. Hydride is not a normal leaving group
in these simple aqueous carbonyl reactions, so aldehyde nucleophilic addition
normally retains its H/carbon substituents. The next unit explains when and
how acyl derivatives undergo substitution rather than just addition.
:::

## Leave with

Two labelled mechanisms, four product-class assignments and an atom-conserving
ring drawing. Optional reading: selected Solomons chapter 16 sections; consult
the [reading guide](../reference/reading.qmd).
